definition.text: A place that is protected because of its recognised natural or cultural value, where human use of resources is limited.

facts.text: The IUCN defines it as a clearly defined space managed, by legal or other effective means, for the long-term conservation of nature and its ecosystem services.
As of 2016 over 161,000 protected areas covered about 17 percent of the world's land surface, excluding Antarctica.
14,688 marine protected areas cover about 10.2% of coastal and marine areas and 4.12% of the global ocean.
Protecting biodiversity in them also protects ecosystem services such as water, fuel, carbon sequestration and climate regulation.
Under Article 8 of the Biodiversity Convention, parties agreed to establish a system of protected areas.
Protecting places is not new: over 2000 years ago royal decrees in India protected certain areas.
New restrictions can displace local people, souring relations with conservationists and sometimes driving poaching.

title: IUCN protected area categories
article: Protected area#IUCN Protected Area Management Categories

definition.text: Six categories, set by the IUCN's World Commission on Protected Areas, that classify protected areas by their management objectives.

facts.text: They provide international standards for defining protected areas and are recognised by many governments and the UN.
They range from Category Ia, strict nature reserve, and Category II, national park, to Category VI, protected areas with sustainable use of natural resources.

definition.text: How well protected areas actually prevent biodiversity loss, judged for example by comparing populations inside and outside them.

facts.text: Vertebrate populations declined about five times more slowly inside protected areas (−0.4% per year) than at similar unprotected sites (−1.8% per year).
Effectiveness is limited by small size, isolation, high costs and growing conflict with human demands for resources.
Only 18% of the area covered by protected areas has been assessed, so most of them have unclear effectiveness.

definition.text: The UN goal 'Climate action': to take urgent action to limit climate change and adapt to its impacts.

facts.text: It has five targets for 2030, including strengthening resilience to climate disasters and building climate measures into national policy.
Target 13.a refers to developed countries' commitment to mobilise $100 billion a year by 2020 for developing countries.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement nations agreed to keep warming well under 2 °C, but pledges would still lead to about 2.7 °C by 2100.
Indicator 13.2.1 counts countries with nationally determined contributions and adaptation plans.
COVID-19 cut 2020 emissions about 6% below projections, but the fall was only temporary.
Critics say it overlooks climate migration as an adaptive response.

definition.text: A global conservation target to halt, or significantly slow, the decline of biodiversity by the end of 2010.

facts.text: EU leaders first adopted it at Gothenburg in June 2001; in 2002 the CBD's COP 6 committed to a significant reduction in the rate of biodiversity loss by 2010.
The 2002 Johannesburg World Summit on Sustainable Development confirmed the target.
Measuring the rate of biodiversity loss to check the target proved a challenge.
The world largely failed to meet it; 2010's 110 national reports showed little progress.
